requirements.requirement: Configure /srv/drop as a shared writable directory where ordinary users cannot remove files owned by other users.
requirements.summary: The directory was created as root:root with mode 1777. Two unprivileged accounts each created files, both cross-user deletion attempts were denied, and each owner could delete its own file. After a verified reboot, mode 1777 and the same behavior were observed again, with test artifacts cleaned up.

requirements.requirement: Keep the installed operating-system release and kernel, using software compatible with the legacy platform.
requirements.summary: CentOS 5.11 and kernel 2.6.18-398.el5 were observed before configuration and remained unchanged after configuration and reboot. The implementation used native filesystem permissions and installed no additional software.

overall_summary: Both material task outcomes are satisfied. The provider-wide restart protocol is also strong: it records the healthy pre-restart directory state and boot ID, restart scheduling, an observed outage, a different post-restart boot ID, and recovered directory state and behavior. Fixed lifecycle boot identities independently agree with the executor evidence.
limitations: The legacy host does not support the lifecycle collector's systemd failed-unit check, so no systemd health comparison is available; no task service or cluster component was involved.

The lifecycle package-health probe invoked an unsupported yum command both before and after execution, so package consistency was not independently established. However, the trace shows no package-management mutations, and direct observations confirm the OS release and kernel remained unchanged.

operational_hygiene.summary: All substantive mutations—creating /srv/drop, setting ownership and mode, creating bounded permission probes, cleaning those probes, and rebooting for the mandatory restart protocol—had clear roles and were appropriately scoped. The one unnecessary retained mutation was /tmp/antrieb-reboot.log, created by the reboot scheduling command and still present afterward; it was not cleaned up. The failed SSH checks during reboot were read-only availability probes and caused no demonstrated mutation.
